newsitem.title: UK: STERLING DOWN AS RATES SEEN PEAKING ON BOE NEWS.
newsitem.headline: STERLING DOWN AS RATES SEEN PEAKING ON BOE NEWS.

text.p: Sterling stumbled over 1-1/2 pfennigs and one cent to below 3.0 marks and $1.60 after the Bank of England hiked rates by 1/4 point to 7.0 percent and signalled they have reached levels consistent with inflation targets, said traders.

"Sterling is coming off because the market is seeing this as possibly the last rate move for a while," said Lee Ferridge, currency strategist at Commerzbank. He said the Bank's comment that rates are now consistent with the government's inflation target reinforced this view and weighed on the pound.

At 1130 GMT sterling/mark was trading at 3.0023/28 against 3.0120/30 marks ahead of the news and 3.0130 in late Europe on Wednesday. It was off troughs of 2.9952 marks, however, hit after the BoE announcement.
Cable was trading at $1.5968/78 against $1.6010 ahead of the rate news and $1.6038 in late Europe on Wednesday. It was off lows of $1.5910 hit after the BoE announcement.

The BoE's Monetary Policy Committee raised official interest rates to 7.0 percent from 6.75 percent on Thursday, the fourth increase in as many months. The BoE also said rates have reached levels consistent with inflation targets of 2.5 percent.

"In the light of the prospect for domestic demand and on the basis of all the evidence currently available, the committee judges that today's rise is necessary to put the economy on track for achieving the inflation target of 2.5 percent looking two years ahead," the committee said in a statement.

Peter Wood, trader at Bank of Boston, said the BoE's comments on sterling also weighed. "Upward pressures on the exchange rate should be reduced by the perception that interest rates have reached a level consistent with the inflation target," the BoE said.
Wood said this reinforced perceptions of rates now on hold.
"They won't be too eager to put interest rates up soon...Unless the economy expands faster or inflation becomes problematic," said Bank of Boston's Wood.
But while traders and analysts saw rates temporarily on hold, they said the pace of economic growth and domestic demand means they have by no means peaked.

"Markets believe we will have a break from rate increases--which we probably will do for a couple of months now. But there is enough in here that we will see higher rates by the end of the year. I still think we will see 7.50 percent by year-end," said Commerzbank's Ferridge.
With expectations of more rate rises quelled, sterling - which has gained from this premise and soared to around eight-year highs of 3.0878 marks in late July - is now under the hammer.
"The view the market has taken is that this is it, pretty much, for rates," said Francis Breedon, senior foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers.

Sterling has crumbled over nine pfennigs to below 3.0 marks since Wednesday. The selloff was triggered on Wednesday when market perceptions shifted in favour of the BoE leaving rates unchanged at 6.75 percent - cable fell to five-month lows as stops were hit and technical levels triggered. By 1300 GMT, cable had stumbled by over four cents to below $1.60
